sources.title: Online Courts and the Future of Justice
sources.author: Richard Susskind
sources.locator: Publisher abstract, especially paragraphs 1 and 3; table of contents, Part II: Is Court a Service or a Place?
sources.verification: Publisher abstract and contents read directly; full book not claimed to have been read.
sources.supports: Susskind frames court reform around access to justice and a service/place question; his account includes online adjudication by human judges.

sources.title: Corrected oral evidence: Constitutional implications of Covid-19
sources.author: Richard Susskind (testimony)
sources.issuer: UK House of Lords, Select Committee on the Constitution
sources.locator: Q30, Susskind’s final answer; contextual qualifications in Q23–24 and Q29.
sources.supports: Susskind distinguishes improving existing processes from using technology to organise work differently; this is a reform argument, not evidence of present AI reliability.

sources.title: Technology and the Future of the Courts
sources.author: James Allsop
sources.issuer: Federal Court of Australia; lecture at the TC Beirne School of Law, University of Queensland
sources.locator: Printed pp. 2–4 (judicial power, human institutions, criticism of the binary service/place framing); pp. 11–12 (limits of efficiency and metrics).
sources.supports: A court’s public judicial function and humanity cannot be reduced to a service/place binary or to performance statistics.

sources.title: Bundesverfassung / Constitution fédérale / Costituzione federale (SR 101)
sources.locator: Art. 29 Abs. 1–2; Art. 29a; Art. 30 Abs. 1 and 3; Art. 191c. Official XML eIds art_29, art_29_a, art_30, art_191_c.
sources.verification: Official Fedlex metadata freshly confirms that consolidation 2024-03-03 applies on 2026-10-09 (dateApplicability 2024-03-03; dateEndApplicability 2028-12-31; next listed consolidation begins 2029-01-01). Art. 29, 29a, 30 and 191c freshly read in the directly fetched official DE/FR/IT XML of that applicable consolidation.
sources.supports: Fair procedure and reasonable time; right to be heard; judicial access subject to exceptional statutory exclusions; lawful competent independent impartial court; public hearing and judgment subject to statutory exceptions; judicial independence and commitment to law.
sources.rights_note: Official legislative text; public-domain legal authority.

sources.title: BGE 129 I 232, judgment 1P.1/2003
sources.verification: Official judgment retrieved directly by HTTPS; E. 3.2 checked against original HTML.
sources.supports: Right to be heard entails serious consideration of submissions and reasons enabling the person concerned and reviewing court to understand and challenge a decision. Judgment arose in a naturalisation-initiative dispute; only its stated general procedural principle is used.
